Pancreatic Masses

Slide 49
Slide 50
Slide 51
Slide 52Pancreatic Masses
  • Pancreatic Pseudocyst.
    • Benign mass
    • Complication of pancreatitis
    • Treated only if symptomatic.
  • NeuroEndocrine Tumors (PNET):
    • Rare, Low grade malignant tumors.
    • 60% are non-functional or non-secretory, which they are more malignant.
    • Can occur in duodenum and peri-pancreatic tissue, gastric, colon and other.
    • Vast majority found accidentally.
Notes

Pancreatic Masses

RELEVANT ANATOMY
The celiac axis gives rise to the common hepatic, splenic, and left gastric arteries. Pancreatic arterial supply includes branches from the gastroduodenal artery (GDA) and the SMA; these vessels run along/behind the gland, which is why their involvement determines tumor resectability in adenocarcinoma.
Notes

Overview of Pancreatic Masses

Pancreatic masses span benign, cystic, neuroendocrine, and malignant lesions.

LesionTypeKey Point
AdenocarcinomaSolid, malignant~90% of solid pancreatic lesions — assume malignant until proven otherwise
PseudocystBenign cysticRelated to pancreatitis
PNETSolid, low-grade malignantUncommon; variable hormone secretion; characteristically hypervascular
⚠ DO NOT MISS
Any pancreatic mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise and warrants urgent surgical/oncology referral.
Any pancreatic mass is malignant until proven otherwise → urgent surgical/oncology referral.

PNET

Slide 53
  • Non-Functional Tumors
    • Asymptomatic, no secretory functions.
    • Usually found incidentally
    • Symptoms arise from mass effect ( abdo pain +/- Jaundice)
    • Diagnosis:
      • Serum chromogranin-A (CGA)
      • 24-hour urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
Notes

Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (PNETs) — General Features

Can arise in the pancreas or other sites: duodenum, peripancreatic tissue, stomach, colon, lungs.
≈60% are non-functional (no clinically significant hormone secretion).
Many are asymptomatic / incidental findings on imaging done for another reason.
Symptoms are usually vague, occurring once the tumor is large enough for mass effect (pain, nausea/vomiting, compression).
A large tumor with few symptoms is concerning — diagnosis is often delayed.
Biochemical work-up: serum chromogranin A, 24-h urinary 5-HIAA when appropriate.
PREOPERATIVE PREP
Non-functional PNETs require no hormone-specific preoperative preparation.
Notes

Functional PNETs

Functional tumors secrete hormones, so symptoms can be severe despite very small tumor size — unlike non-functional tumors (usually incidental), functional PNETs typically present because of their hormonal syndrome. Biologic behavior varies widely: insulinoma is the most benign / best survival, while somatostatinoma is among the most aggressive / lowest survival.

Slide 54PNET
  • Non-Functional PENT management :
    • No specific pre-operative preparation.
    • Size > 2 cm or with malignant features =======> surgical resection
    • Size 1-2 cm ===> in selected pt with high risk surgical candidates, depending not the site of the tumor > can be observed or resected
    • Size < 1 cm ===> can be observed , and if elected to be removed ==> surgical enucleation can be done .
    • The overall 5-year survival for non-functional pancreatic endocrine tumors is approximately 30-50%.
Notes

Non-Functional PNET — Management by Size

SizeApproach
< 1 cmUsually observation; selected small lesions may undergo enucleation (remove only the mass, not a formal resection)
1–2 cmIndividualized — weigh age, comorbidities, location, operative risk, life expectancy, and reliability of follow-up. Elderly/high-risk → observe; young/healthy → often favor resection (lifetime growth/metastasis risk, possible loss to follow-up)
> 2 cm or malignant-lookingGenerally surgical resection
REMEMBER
PNETs retain the ability to metastasize even when relatively indolent. Quoted overall survival after resection ≈ 30–50%.
Slide 55
Slide 56PNET
  • Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN I)
    • AD hereditary syndrome.
    • 80% develop hyperparathyroidism.
    • 80-100% will develop PNET
    • 50% will develop gastrinoma’s
    • most will have multiple types.
  • VHL
    • 10-17% will develop PNET, 98% are non-functional.
Notes

PNET-Associated Hereditary Syndromes

SyndromeAssociation
MEN (1)Strong association with hyperparathyroidism; may have multiple PNETs — gastrinomas are common
Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL)≈20% develop PNETs; most are non-functional

Functional PNET

Slide 57

PNET

Slide 58
  • Localization:
    • CT/MRI
      • usually hypervascualr, non-functional usually lager is size, insulinomas and gastronomes are smaller.
    • SRS/Octeriotide scan:
      • The abundance of somatostatin receptors on certain of pancreatic endocrine tumors ( well differentiated G1,G2)
    • FDG-PET scan :
      • Positive for high grade tumors (G3).
Slide 59PNET
  • EUS +FNA:
    • is more sensitive than CT &MRI for detecting tumors < 3cm
    • FNA for Ki67
  • Other means of localisation :
    • Angiography, portal veinous sampling and arterial stimulation.
    • As last resort : Surgical exploration
Notes

Localization / Imaging Work-Up

1. CT / MRI — first-line; PNETs are characteristically hypervascular with intense arterial enhancement.

2. Somatostatin-receptor imaging / Octreotide scan — detects tumors expressing somatostatin receptors. 3. PET scan — particularly useful for more aggressive/high-grade tumors.

4. Endoscopy — gastroscopy when relevant; ERCP if a biliary-region lesion is suspected.

5. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) — very useful especially for small lesions; allows biopsy/FNA and grading (e.g. Ki-67). 6. Other: angiography (increased tumor blood supply), arterial stimulation + venous sampling, surgical exploration as a last resort.

HIGH YIELD
PNETs are typically hypervascular — this is the key imaging distinction from adenocarcinoma (see High-Yield Comparisons, end of guide).
GRADE
PNETs range from well-differentiated to poorly differentiated / high-grade. Grade 3 tumors behave like conventional aggressive cancer/adenocarcinoma → systemic chemotherapy may be required.

Functional PNET

Slide 60
  • Insulinomas:
    • Most common functional tumor, most commonly benign.
    • Secrets Pro-Insulin —-> Insulin ——> C-peptide
    • Whipple’s triad: fasting-induced neuroglyopenic symptoms of hypoglycemia (diaphoresis, shaking, mental confusion, obtundation, and seizures), low blood glucose levels (40 to 50 mg/dL), and relief of symptoms after the administration of glucose.
    • Diagnosis:
      • C-peptide levels + insulin/glucose ratio ( >0.3)
    • Treatment :
      • local resection/enucleation.
  • Hypoglycaemia relieved by juice + pancreatic tail mass → confirm insulinoma with high C-peptide (insulin/glucose ratio > 0.3). 436 ×2
Slide 61Functional PNET
  • Gastrinoma:
    • most found in duodenum, produces Zollinger Ellison Syndrome. (Gastrinoma triangle )
    • ZES consists of hypergastrinemia, subsequent severe peptic ulceration ( recurrent severe abdominal pain) and, often, severe diarrhea.
    • Adult pancreas has no Gastrin production, normal in G-cell in the antrum.
    • Diagnosis
      • Fasting serum Gastrin > 1000 pg/ml.
      • EGD
    • Treatment:
      • Hypersecretion controlled by PPI
      • Surgical resection due to high chance of mets.
  • Recurrent ulcers resistant to PPI, markedly high fasting gastrin, diarrhoea → Zollinger–Ellison syndrome 442 ×2; commonest site of gastrinoma outside the pancreas → duodenum. 441
Slide 62Functional PNET
Slide 63Functional PNET
  • (Vasoactive Intestinal peptide )VIPomas:
    • high levels of VIP, called Verner-Morrison syndrome.
    • Profuse watery, iso-osmotic secretory diarrhea ( persists despite fasting) is the most common presenting symptom and may exceed a volume of 3 to 5 liters/day, leading to HypoKalemia and acidosis.
    • Diagnosis:
      • high plasma level of VIP > 1000 pg/ml
    • Treatment:
      • Surgical resection.
Slide 64Functional PNET
  • Glucagonomas:
    • Tend to be larger in size , around 5-10 cm.
    • Presents with 4 Ds : diabetes, dermatitis, DVT, and depression.
    • necrolytic migratory erythema is due to AA def, if given , it improves.
    • Diagnosis
      • A fasting glucagon level >1000 pg/mL ( normal < = 50)
    • Treatment:
      • Improve nutritional condition
      • Agressive resection.
Notes

Functional PNET Syndromes — Comparison

TumorClassic Syndrome / PresentationDiagnostic ClueKey NotesManagement
InsulinomaHypoglycemia; symptoms relieved by glucoseWhipple's triad; insulin/glucose ratio > 0.3; ↑C-peptideMost benign functional PNET; best survivalSmall (~1 cm), away from duct → enucleation possible
GastrinomaZollinger–Ellison: multiple/recurrent peptic ulcers, abdominal pain, ± diarrheaFasting gastrin > 1,000Arises in gastrinoma triangle (pancreas / duodenum / CBD region)High-dose PPI preop → surgical resection if resectable
VIPomaVerner–Morrison: massive watery diarrhea, 4–6 L/day+↑ Plasma VIP; diarrhea continues despite fastingSevere fluid/electrolyte loss → dehydration, acidosis, ± AKISurgical resection
Glucagonoma4 Ds: Diabetes, Dermatitis, DVT, DepressionFasting glucagon > 1,000 (normal < 50)Tend to be larger; characteristic necrolytic migratory erythema (nutritional/amino-acid deficiency)Correct nutrition first → aggressive resection
SomatostatinomaDiarrhea, diabetes, other GI/metabolic disturbanceFasting somatostatin > 100Very rare; among the most aggressive PNETsOptimize nutrition → aggressive resection
WHIPPLE'S TRIAD (INSULINOMA)
1) Symptoms/signs of hypoglycemia · 2) Documented low plasma glucose (usually < 55 mg/dL) at time of symptoms · 3) Relief of symptoms after glucose administration.
RASH PATTERN-RECOGNITION
Necrolytic migratory erythema on the exam = think glucagonoma. It may improve with nutritional/amino-acid replacement.
Slide 65Functional PNET
  • Somatostatinomas:
    • very rare, usually solitary.
    • The full syndrome of steatorrhea, diabetes , hypochlorhydria, and gallstones
    • Diagnosis:
      • Fasting somatostatin > 100 pg/mL
    • Treatment:
      • Improve nutritional condition
      • Agressive resection.

PNET

Slide 66
  • Principles of treatment
    • Mainstay of treatment is surgery.
    • Octeriotide may be used to improve symptoms.
    • Role of liver mets debulking.
    • Systemic therapy ( chemo +/- biological agents ) : in case of non operative metastatic disease and/ or progressing PNET.
  • High recurrence rate : it requires close clinical and radiological follow up.
Notes

General Treatment of Functional PNETs

SURGERY
Main definitive treatment when resectable.
OCTREOTIDE
Octreotide / somatostatin analogue markedly reduces hormone-mediated symptoms. Long-acting monthly preparations can control severe diarrhea, ulcer symptoms, etc.
METASTATIC PNET — DEBULKING
Unlike adenocarcinoma, metastatic PNET may still benefit from surgical debulking (liver = most common first metastatic site). Removing bulk tumor even without complete resection can markedly reduce hormone secretion and improve symptoms, quality of life, and potentially survival. Systemic/biologic therapy may also be used. PNETs may recur locally despite negative margins, reflecting aggressive underlying biology.

Pancreatic Cystic Lesions

Slide 67
  • Serous Cystadenoma:
    • Benign, low probability of malignant transformation ( cystadenocarcinoma).
    • Mostly asymptomatic , but may presents with vague abdo pain, may be wtt loss and jaundice ( mass effect symptoms, more likely > 4 cm )
    • Diagnosis:
      • CT scan: large, well circumscribed masses, with central calcification/scar and radiating septa ( sunburst appearance) with clusters of small cysts, a “honeycomb” appearance. (hypervascular)
      • EUS and FNA ( Unilocular mass) with cyst fluid shows low levels of amylase, CA 19-9 , CEA, acellular with no mucin and no malignant cells.
    • Treatment :
      • Surgical resection ONLY if symptomatic.
Slide 68
Slide 69Pancreatic Cystic Lesions
  • Mucinous Cystadenoma:
    • They span from benign to malignant ( 40% at Dx)
    • Both Mucin and serous are much more common in females.
    • Symptoms of mass effect , may be pancreatitis.
    • Diagnosis :
      • CT scan is the presence of a solitary cyst, which may have fine septations
        • Presence of calcification, large tumor size ( or change in size), or a mural nodule is suggestive of malignancy.
      • EUS and FNA with cyst fluid : mucin rich fluid, high CEA levels, low or high amylase.
Notes

Pancreatic Cystic Lesions

Three major lesions: serous cystadenoma, mucinous cystic neoplasm (MCN), and IPMN.

PATTERN RECOGNITION
Mucin → think malignant potential. Serous fluid is bland/benign; mucinous fluid (MCN, IPMN) carries real malignant risk.
Serous CystadenomaMucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN)IPMN
Malignant potentialVery low (rare cystadenocarcinoma)~40–50%Important — up to ~80% for main-duct
Typical patientUsually asymptomatic, any sexMore common in females, usually solitaryAssociated with duct dilatation
Duct communicationNoNo communication with pancreatic ductYes — communicates with duct (key distinguishing feature)
ImagingClassic honeycomb appearanceSeptations, calcification, large cystic componentsDuct dilatation ± mural nodules
Cyst fluidBland / non-mucinousThick mucinous; low amylase & low glucose; high CEAMucinous; high amylase; high CEA
TreatmentResect only if symptomaticResect regardless of size (high malignant potential)Depends on type/size — see below
WHY THE AMYLASE DIFFERS
MCN does not communicate with the pancreatic duct → low amylase/glucose in cyst fluid. IPMN communicates with the duct → high amylase in cyst fluid. This single fact resolves most exam questions distinguishing the two.
Slide 70Pancreatic Cystic Lesions
  • Mucinous Cystadenoma:
  • Diagnosis confirmation requires pathological examination which shows ovarian like stroma.
  • Treatment: Surgical resection.
  • Prognosis depends on invasiveness, invasive pathology has 5-yr survival around 60% (Slightly better than PDAC).
  • might require adjuvant chemo.
  • Requires close clinical and radiological follow up
Slide 71Pancreatic Cystic Lesions
  • Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasm( IPMN):
    • Group of lesions characterized by a papillary growth of the ductal epithelium with rich mucin production and cystic expansion of the affected duct.
    • It differs from MCN because of a direct communication with the Wirsung duct and the absence of ovarian-type stroma.
    • IPMNs are further characterized by the extent to which they involve the pancreatic ducts.

IPMN

Slide 72
  • Main duct IMPN:
    • abnormal duct dilatation of the MD with columnar metaplasia.
    • malignant transformation found in 60-80% of the time
    • Abdo pain, wtt loss, acute pancreatitis, jaundice.
    • MD > 10 mm high risk
    • Diagnosis:
      • CT, MRI, EUS + FNA ( also high in CEA levels)
    • Treatment :
      • Surgical resection
Slide 73
Slide 74IPMN
  • Side Branch IPMN:
    • abnormal duct dilatation of side duct branch connected to MD
    • Malignant transformation is correlated with size.
    • Features that predict risk of malignancy : mural nodules or thickening of the wall, enhancing solid component within the cyst, progressing in size.
    • Some clinical symptoms also including jaundice, pain, and diabetes.
    • Diagnosis:
      • CT , MRI
      • EUS + FNA
Notes

IPMN Subtypes

TypeFeatures
Main-duct IPMNDirectly involves the main pancreatic duct → dilatation + mucin production. Very high malignant risk (~80%). Risk rises with duct diameter. Normal duct ≈2–3 mm; duct ≈10 mm = very high risk. May present with pain, weight loss, ± jaundice. Diagnosis: CT, MRI/MRCP, EUS. Aspirate shows mucin, high amylase, high CEA. Treatment: surgical resection.
Side-branch IPMNArises from a side branch rather than the main duct. Malignant potential correlates with cyst size and high- risk imaging features: mural nodule, enhancing solid component, progressive increase in size. Small lesions are commonly incidental.
Mixed typeBoth main-duct and side-branch involvement may occur — treat with the higher-risk (main-duct) approach.
  • Incidental IPMN with main-duct dilatation 12 mm → surgical resection (distal pancreatectomy). 436
Slide 75

SB-IPMN

Slide 76
  • Management:
    • If Asymptomatic side branch and the size < 1 cm ==> CT/MRI yearly.
    • If Asymptomatic side branch and the size 1-3 cm ==> repeat image in 6 months for 2 years then yearly.
    • Surgical resection because increase risk of malignancy for the following:
      • Any size SB symptomatic with worrisome imaging features.
      • If side branch size > 3cm
      • Main Duct or Mixed type IPMN
  • 5- year Survival with invasive Cancer is around 50-60%
  • No role for adjuvant chemo.
  • Asymptomatic 70-year-old, incidental 2.5-cm side-branch IPMN, main duct normal → CT every 6 months. 437
Notes

Side-Branch IPMN — Surveillance (Asymptomatic)

SizeSurveillance Interval
< 1 cmCT/MRI yearly
1–3 cmCT/MRI ~every 6 months initially, then yearly
SURGICAL INDICATIONS — SIDE-BRANCH IPMN
Symptoms · high-risk malignant features (mural nodule, enhancing solid component, rapid growth) · size > 3 cm · mixed-type IPMN.
NUMBERS TO REMEMBER
Main duct: 10 mm = high risk. Side branch: 3 cm = key surgical threshold.
AFTER RESECTION
If pathology shows only IPMN/dysplasia without invasive carcinoma (low/intermediate/high-grade) → no chemotherapy needed for non-invasive IPMN. If a focus of invasive adenocarcinoma is found, treat per pancreatic adenocarcinoma guidelines.
Slide 77

Adenocarcinoma

Slide 78
  • Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
    • Most common pancreatic mass, around 90% of all masses
    • Risk Factors:
      • Smoking, diabetes, obesity , C. pancreatitis and AGE (>50 yrs).
      • Hereditary associations with : BRCA 2, cystic fibrosis, lynch syndrome, Peutz- Jeghers syndrome ( highest), FAP and other.
    • Usually late presentation, symptoms depend on the location :
      • jaundice, wtt loss, abdo pain, N&V
Slide 79Adenocarcinoma
  • Investigation
    • Ca 19-9 most sensitive and specific tumor marker.
      • Can be falsely elevated in hyperbilirubinemia
    • Triphasic CT and/or MRI/MRCP with have high sensitivity.
      • Hypoattenuation, PD dilatation, CBD dilatation , DD sign
    • PET scan
    • ERCP and brushing
    • EUS +/- FNA
Notes

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma

The most important pancreatic malignancy — ≈90% of solid pancreatic lesions; highly aggressive with generally poor prognosis. Risk factors: increasing age, smoking. Often presents late with jaundice, weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting.

CA 19-9 PITFALL
CA 19-9 is the major tumor marker used, but it can be falsely elevated in obstructive jaundice/hyperbilirubinemia. Relieve/normalize biliary obstruction first, then reassess CA 19-9. Do not interpret a markedly elevated CA 19-9 blindly in a jaundiced patient.
Notes

Imaging

LesionVascularity
PNETHypervascular — intense arterial enhancement
AdenocarcinomaHypovascular / hypoattenuating / hypodense
DOUBLE-DUCT SIGN — VERY BAD SIGN
Dilated pancreatic duct + dilated CBD = double-duct sign → highly suspicious for pancreatic head malignancy. Other work-up: PET, ERCP + brush cytology, EUS ± biopsy.
IS TISSUE DIAGNOSIS REQUIRED BEFORE SURGERY?
Unlike breast/colon tumors, preoperative tissue diagnosis is not always required for a clearly resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma. ERCP brushing/biopsy has relatively low yield (quoted ≈20–30%), and repeated attempts can significantly delay definitive treatment. If the clinical picture + imaging + tumor markers are highly characteristic and the lesion is resectable → proceed directly to surgery. Do not delay potentially curative surgery solely for repeated unsuccessful biopsy attempts.
Double-duct sign (dilated pancreatic duct + CBD) → pancreatic head malignancy.
  • Tumour marker for pancreatic head tumour → CA 19-9. 436
Slide 80Adenocarcinoma
  • Management :
    • Tissue diagnosis is NOT need for upfront surgery.
    • Depending on the location, invasion and mets
      • No role of surgery in metastatic disease
      • Pancreatic head : Whipple’s procedure
      • pancreatic body and tail : distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy
  • Adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head → pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple). 436
Notes

Surgery by Tumor Location

LocationProcedure
Head of pancreasWhipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy)
Body / tailDistal pancreatectomy + splenectomy — generally less morbid than Whipple; spleen removed for oncologic regional lymphadenectomy
Notes

Whipple Procedure — Structures

Removed: head of pancreas
Uncinate process
Duodenum
Distal bile duct / CBD region
Reconstruction: pancreaticojejunostomy
Hepaticojejunostomy
Gastrojejunostomy

Large en-bloc resection is necessary due to shared blood supply and lymphatic drainage in the pancreatic head/duodenal region.

Slide 81
Slide 82
Slide 83Adenocarcinoma
  • Pancreatic head tumor
    • can be divided into 3 categories: resectable, borderline and non-resectable
      • Borderline resectable tumors defined as :
        • 1. Severe unilateral or bilateral SMV-portal impingement.
        • 2. SMV occlusion, if of a short segment, and reconstructible.
        • 3. Less than 180-degree tumor abutment on the SMA.
        • 4. Abutment or encasement of hepatic artery (not the bifurcation), if reconstructible.
    • High morbidity and mortality operation.
Notes

Resectability

CategoryVascular Criteria
ResectableNo significant SMV/portal-vein or major arterial involvement
Borderline resectableSignificant uni/bilateral SMV/portal-vein impingement; short-segment venous occlusion if reconstructable; encasement ≤180°; selected hepatic-artery involvement if reconstruction is feasible
UnresectableMore extensive vascular encasement (e.g. >180°), especially if reconstruction is not feasible
CORE CONCEPT
Resectability depends not only on whether a vessel is involved, but on whether involved vessels can be safely reconstructed.
Slide 84Adenocarcinoma
  • Pancreatic body and tail tumors:
    • late presentation, carry worse prognosis
    • less morbidity and mortality rate than whipple.
  • Role of Chemo and radiation:
    • all pt must receive chemo therapy in form of adjuvant or neoadjuvant to improve survival.
      • Gemcitabine or 5-FU with leucovorin or FOLFIRINOX
    • Pt with unresectable or border line resectable are candidates to receive chemo-radation therapy
      • FOLFIRINOX or Gemcitabine + Paclitaxel + RT
      • If surgery planned , should be 6-8 wks after NeoAdj
Notes

Head vs. Body/Tail — Presentation

Behavior
HeadOften symptomatic earlier — causes biliary obstruction → jaundice
Body / tailCan remain clinically silent for a long time → frequently presents at a more advanced stage; poorer prognosis
METASTATIC DISEASE
Unlike PNETs, there is generally no role for curative pancreatic resection in metastatic adenocarcinoma. Systemic disease → systemic therapy, not resection.
  • 67-year-old, painless progressive jaundice, palpable gallbladder → carcinoma of the head of the pancreas 438 ×9; Courvoisier's law → palpable gallbladder: jaundice unlikely to be due to a stone. 429 ×2
Notes

Chemotherapy / Chemoradiation

Generally requires systemic chemotherapy — neoadjuvant (before surgery) or adjuvant (after).
Unresectable/metastatic disease → chemotherapy for systemic/palliative treatment.
Borderline resectable: increasing preference for neoadjuvant chemotherapy to improve resectability, assess tumor biology/chemosensitivity, and select patients likely to benefit from surgery.
Tumors that respond well to chemo tend to have more favorable biology/outcomes.
If surgery follows chemo/radiation, allow ≈6–8 weeks for recovery before operating.
Slide 85Adenocarcinoma
  • Obstructive cancer and metastatic cancer
    • 40-50 % present with metastasis.
    • Might have exocrine and /or endocrine malfunction with or without surgery.
    • CBD obstruction : stent or HJ bypass
    • Gastric outlet obstruction : Gastrojejunosotmy bypass
    • Palliative CT/RT may be of value
    • 5-yr survival with complete resection and chemo around 15-35%
Notes

Pancreatic Functional Insufficiency

TypeManifestation / Treatment
EndocrineDiabetes mellitus
ExocrineDiarrhea, steatorrhea → treat with pancreatic enzyme supplementation
Can result from the tumor itself or after pancreatic surgery.
UNEXPECTED METASTASES AT SURGERY
If metastatic disease is found intraoperatively in a patient thought to have resectable disease → abort curative resection. Avoid a major operation that only delays effective systemic chemotherapy.
Notes

Palliation of Obstruction

ApproachOptions
SurgicalPalliative biliary bypass; gastric bypass
EndoscopicBiliary/CBD stent; enteral/duodenal stenting
Prefer endoscopic options where possible — avoid unnecessary major surgery, since postoperative recovery can delay chemotherapy.
PROGNOSIS
One of the most aggressive malignancies. Even in the best scenario — localized disease, complete resection, full adjuvant chemotherapy — quoted 5-year survival is only ≈35%.

Other diseases

Slide 86
  • Solid pseudopapillary tumors:
    • SPTs are infrequent, mostly benign tumors of the pancreas, commonly in young women ( 22-38 yrs).
    • SPTs are distinct in having both solid and cystic components
    • Treatment is surgery EVEN in metastatic disease.
  • Mets to the pancreas:
    • 60% from RCC.
    • Nearly 50% of patients with metastatic tumors to the pancreas are Asymptomatic.
    • Hypervascular lesions of the pancreas are more likely to be metastatic rather than primary pancreatic carcinoma.
    • Every case is different , RCC benefit from surgery.
  • Hypervascular pancreatic tail lesion years after RCC resection → distal pancreatectomy. 437
Notes

Other Pancreatic Lesions

Solid Pseudopapillary Tumor

Occurs predominantly in young females. Characteristic imaging/pathology shows a mixed solid + cystic component. Generally indolent/low-grade but can metastasize. Even with metastatic disease, surgical resection may still be beneficial.

Notes

Metastases to the Pancreas

The pancreas can receive metastases from several cancers, including melanoma, breast cancer, and others. Management depends on primary tumor biology, extent of disease, patient condition, and expected survival.

RENAL CELL CARCINOMA (RCC)
≈60% of pancreatic metastases arise from RCC. These are often asymptomatic/incidental and usually hypervascular. Unlike many metastatic cancers, selected RCC metastases to the pancreas benefit from pancreatic resection, which may improve survival.
Notes

High-Yield Comparisons

DistinctionAnswer
PNET vs. Adenocarcinoma (imaging)PNET = hypervascular; Adenocarcinoma = hypovascular/hypodense
MCNMucinous, usually female, no duct communication, low amylase → resect regardless of size (high malignant potential)
IPMNMucinous, communicates with duct, high amylase
Main-duct IPMNMalignancy risk very high; 10 mm duct = high risk
Side-branch IPMN>3 cm / mural nodule / enhancing solid component / growth / symptoms → consider resection
InsulinomaMost benign functional PNET; hypoglycemia + Whipple's triad
GastrinomaZollinger–Ellison; fasting gastrin >1,000
VIPomaSevere watery diarrhea despite fasting
Glucagonoma4 Ds + necrolytic migratory erythema
SomatostatinomaVery rare; fasting level >100
Head adenocarcinomaJaundice earlier → Whipple
Body/tail adenocarcinomaSilent/late → distal pancreatectomy + splenectomy
Double-duct signPancreatic duct + CBD dilatation → strongly suspicious for pancreatic head malignancy
Metastatic adenocarcinomaSystemic therapy; generally no curative resection
Metastatic PNETDebulking may still improve symptoms/survival
RCC → pancreas metastasisSelected patients may benefit from pancreatic resection
Notes

Mastery Checklist
dug:
Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms
Head of Pancreas Tumors (More Common, Earlier Diagnosis)
  • Painless jaundice (biliary obstruction).
  • Weight loss & anorexia (~80%).
  • Pruritus (due to bile salt accumulation).
  • Dark urine & pale stools (obstructive jaundice).
  • Epigastric pain → Radiates to the back (~25%).
  • Palpable, nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign).
Body/Tail Tumors (More Advanced, Later Diagnosis)
  • Abdominal pain (often severe, radiates to back).
  • Weight loss & cachexia (~80%).
  • Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau’s sign, ~10%).
  • New-onset diabetes (~25%).
B. Signs
  • Jaundice & pruritus (bile duct compression).
  • Palpable epigastric mass (~10%).
  • Hepatomegaly & ascites (liver metastases).
  • Virchow’s node (left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy).
  • Sister Mary Joseph’s nodule (periumbilical metastasis).
  • Blumer’s shelf (rectal shelf mass, peritoneal metastasis).
Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Tests
  • ↑ CA 19-9 (>1000 U/mL highly specific but NOT diagnostic).
  • ↑ Bilirubin & ALP (biliary obstruction).
  • Mild ↑ AST/ALT (liver involvement).
  • ↑ CEA (~60% of cases, nonspecific).
  • Glucose intolerance/new-onset diabetes (~25%).
B. Imaging Studies
CT scan (Initial Test)
  • Multiphase contrast-enhanced pancreatic protocol CT is first-line.
  • Shows pancreatic mass, ductal dilation, vascular invasion, metastases.
MRI/MRCP
  • Alternative for better soft tissue contrast & duct evaluation.
  • Helpful if uncertain diagnosis or allergic to contrast.
EUS + FNA (Endoscopic Ultrasound + Biopsy)
  • Most sensitive test for small tumors (<2 cm).
  • Allows guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) for histologic confirmation.
ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography)
  • Used only if biliary obstruction is unclear.
  • Shows "double duct sign" (dilated pancreatic + common bile duct).
PET-CT
  • Detects occult metastases.
  • Used in staging or suspected metastatic disease.
Laparoscopy
  • Done before surgery to assess for peritoneal spread.
Staging & Resectability
TNM Staging System
  • T1-T2: Confined to pancreas.
  • T3-T4: Invades major vessels or nearby structures.
  • N1-N2: Lymph node involvement.
  • M1: Distant metastases (liver, lung, peritoneum).
Resectability Criteria
  • Resectable: No major vessel invasion or distant metastases.
  • Borderline Resectable: Involves SMV, PV, or hepatic artery (partial contact).
  • Unresectable: Encases SMA, CA, IVC, distant metastases.
Treatment Options
1. Surgical Resection (Only 15-20% of cases)
  • Curative option for localized disease.
  • Whipple Procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy)
  • For tumors in the pancreatic head.
  • Removes head of pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder, CBD, part of stomach/jejunum.
  • Distal Pancreatectomy + Splenectomy
  • For tumors in the body/tail.
  • Total Pancreatectomy (rare, for diffuse disease).
  • Complications: Pancreatic fistula delayed gastric emptying, anastomotic leaks.
2. Neoadjuvant Therapy (For Borderline Resectable Tumors)
  • Chemotherapy ± radiation before surgery to shrink the tumor.
  • Regimens:
  • FOLFIRINOX (most effective but toxic).
  • Gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel (less toxic, well-tolerated).
3. Adjuvant Chemotherapy (Post-Surgery)
  • Gemcitabine ± Capecitabine (Improves survival).
  • FOLFIRINOX (For fit patients, best survival benefit).
4. Palliative Therapy (For Metastatic/Unresectable Tumors)
  • Chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX or Gemcitabine-based regimens).
  • Endoscopic biliary stenting (for obstructive jaundice).
  • Celiac plexus block (for severe pain).
  • Palliative surgery (gastrojejunostomy for gastric outlet obstruction).
  • Radiation therapy (pain control in metastases).
Prognosis
Overall:
  • 5-year survival: ~ 5-10%.
  • If resected + adjuvant therapy: ~ 20-28% (best case).
  • If unresectable/metastatic: Median survival ~7 months.
Poor Prognostic Factors:
  • Lymph node involvement.
  • Tumor size >2.5 cm.
  • Vascular invasion.
  • Poor differentiation.
  • High CA 19-9 levels post-surgery.
Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas
  • Pancreatic cystic neoplasms are often incidental findings on imaging.
  • Rarely symptomatic (abdominal pain, mass, or jaundice).
  • Classified as Mucinous (premalignant/malignant) & non-mucinous (benign).
  • Management depends on size, symptoms, and malignancy risk.

1. Serous Cystadenoma (SCA)
  • Benign, non-mucinous cystic tumor.
  • More common in women (~75%), usually in the 6th-7th decade.
  • "Honeycomb" appearance on imaging (multiple small cysts).
  • Central calcification (pathognomonic but seen in <30%).
  • Slow-growing, rarely symptomatic.
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Multilocular cysts with central calcification.
  • EUS + FNA (if unclear): Low CEA & amylase, glycogen-rich cuboidal epithelium.
Management:
  • Observation unless symptomatic or large (>4 cm).
  • Resection for symptomatic cases (pain, mass effect).
2. Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN)
  • Premalignant mucinous cystic lesion (~30% risk of carcinoma).
  • Occurs exclusively in women (mean age: ~50 years).
  • Does NOT communicate with pancreatic ducts.
  • Most common in pancreatic body/tail.
  • Septated cysts with thick walls on imaging.
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Unilocular or multilocular cyst with septations, no duct communication.
  • EUS + FNA: ↑ CEA (>192 ng/mL), ↑ mucin, variable cytology.
Management:
  • Surgical resection if >3 cm, symptomatic, or has concerning features (thick walls, nodules).
  • Observation for small, asymptomatic MCNs (<3 cm).
3. Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasm (IPMN)
  • Premalignant mucinous tumor arising from pancreatic ducts.
  • More common in men (~60%), typically age >60 years.
  • Can progress to invasive carcinoma.
  • Classified into:
  • Main Duct IPMN (high-risk, always resect).
  • Branch Duct IPMN (lower risk, selective resection).
  • Mixed Type (main + branch duct, high-risk).

4. Cystic Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs)
  • Rare cystic variant of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.
  • Can be functional (hormone-secreting) or non-functional.
  • Seen in MEN-1 syndrome (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1).
  • Malignant potential (require resection).
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Well-defined cystic lesion with enhancing septa.
  • EUS + FNA: Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, high CEA.
  • Hormonal Workup: Insulin, gastrin, glucagon, VIP (if functional).
Management:
  • Surgical resection (due to malignancy risk).
5. Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm (SPN)
  • Rare, low-grade malignant tumor, common in young women (~30-40s).
  • Well-defined cystic mass with solid areas.
  • Slow-growing but may metastasize (low-risk).
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Large, well-circumscribed mass with solid & cystic areas.
  • EUS + FNA: β-catenin mutations, positive for synaptophysin & vimentin.
Management:
  • Surgical resection (curative in >80% of cases).

Adenoma & Adenocarcinoma of the Ampulla of Vater
  • Ampullary tumors account for ~10% of neoplasms causing distal bile duct obstruction.
  • Adenomas are benign but can progress to adenocarcinoma (premalignant).
  • Adenocarcinoma of the ampulla has a better prognosis than pancreatic cancer due to early presentation.
Clinical Presentation
  • Painless jaundice (due to biliary obstruction).
  • Intermittent jaundice & pruritus (from partial obstruction).
  • Weight loss & abdominal pain (if advanced).
  • Occult GI bleeding → Anemia, melena, or hematochezia.
  • Courvoisier’s sign (palpable gallbladder in a jaundiced patient, suggestive of malignancy).
Diagnosis
Imaging
CT scan:
  • Dilated common bile duct & pancreatic duct (Double Duct Sign).
  • Can detect metastases & local invasion.
Ultrasound (US):
  • Can show biliary duct dilation but is limited in detecting ampullary tumors.
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP):
  • Best for direct visualization of ampullary lesions.
  • 75% of cases → Visible mass on duodenoscopy (exophytic, ulcerated, or infiltrating).
  • Biopsy via ERCP confirms diagnosis.
Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS):
  • Evaluate tumor depth & lymph node involvement.
  • Guided biopsy if ERCP biopsy is inconclusive.
Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP):
  • Non-invasive alternative to ERCP (but lacks biopsy capability).
Management
1️- Ampullary Adenoma (Benign, Premalignant)
  • If resectable → Endoscopic or Surgical Removal
  • Endoscopic Resection (for small, non-invasive tumors)
  • Surgical Resection (if not completely removable by endoscopy)
  • Surveillance after resection due to recurrence risk
2️- Ampullary Adenocarcinoma (Malignant)
  • Surgical resection is the only curative treatment
  • Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple Procedure) → Standard treatment for resectable cases.
  • Local Resection → Considered in select early-stage cases without lymph node involvement.
  • Adjuvant Chemotherapy → For advanced tumors or nodal involvement.
  • Unresectable Disease?
  • Palliative ERCP with biliary stenting → To relieve jaundice & symptoms.
  • Palliative Chemotherapy → For metastatic disease.
  • Prognosis: <1 year survival in unresectable cases.
Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (PNETs)
  • Rare tumors (~1–5 cases per million per year).
  • Arise from islet cells of the pancreas (hormone-producing).
  • Classified as:
  • Functioning PNETs → Secrete hormones, causing distinct syndromes.
  • Non-functioning PNETs → Often found incidentally on imaging.
  • Malignancy potential varies (some benign, others aggressive with metastases).
1️- Non-Functioning PNETs
  • Most common subtype (~50-75%).
  • Usually asymptomatic, detected incidentally.
  • If symptomatic → Due to tumor mass effect:
  • Abdominal pain (most common).
  • Weight loss, jaundice, back pain (advanced cases).
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Enhancing pancreatic mass.
  • EUS + Biopsy → Confirm histology & malignancy potential.
  • Chromogranin A, neuron-specific enolase (NSE) → Tumor markers
  • Management:
  • <1 cm → Surveillance.
  • >2 cm or rapid growth → Surgical resection (Whipple for head lesions, distal pancreatectomy for body/tail lesions).
  • Metastatic disease → Consider debulking, chemotherapy, or targeted therapy.
2️- Functioning PNETs (Hormone-Secreting Tumors)
2A. Insulinoma (Most Common Functioning PNET)
  • Secretes Insulin → Severe fasting hypoglycemia.
  • Symptoms (Whipple’s Triad):
  • (1) Fasting or exertional hypoglycemia (<50 mg/dL).
  • (2) Symptoms of neuroglycopenia (confusion, vision changes, syncope).
  • (3) Symptom relief after glucose administration.
  • Diagnosis:
  • 72-hour fasting test → Persistent hypoglycemia with high insulin & C-peptide.
  • Imaging: CT, MRI, EUS (best for small tumors), selective arterial calcium stimulation test.
  • Management:
  • Surgical resection (enucleation if small, distal pancreatectomy or Whipple for larger tumors).
  • Diazoxide (insulin secretion blocker) or octreotide if inoperable.
2B. Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome - ZES)
  • Secretes Gastrin → Hyperacidity & refractory ulcers.
  • Symptoms:
  • Severe peptic ulcers (multiple, recurrent, or resistant to PPIs).
  • Diarrhea & steatorrhea (malabsorption from acid inactivation of pancreatic enzymes).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum gastrin >1000 pg/mL (definitive).
  • Secretin stimulation test (gastrin rises paradoxically).
  • CT/EUS/Somatostatin Receptor Scintigraphy (SRS) for localization.
  • Management:
  • High-dose PPIs (to control acidity).
  • Surgical resection if localized.
  • Metastatic disease → Consider somatostatin analogs, targeted therapy (sunitinib, everolimus).
2C. VIPoma (Pancreatic Cholera - WDHA Syndrome)
  • Secretes Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) → Severe watery diarrhea (>3L/day), dehydration, & hypokalemia.
  • Symptoms:
  • Watery diarrhea (profuse, secretory, persists with fasting).
  • Hypokalemia & metabolic acidosis (HCO3 loss in stool).
  • Achlorhydria (low stomach acid production).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum VIP >75 pg/mL.
  • CT/MRI/EUS for tumor localization.
  • Management:
  • Somatostatin analogs (octreotide) (reduces diarrhea).
  • Surgical resection if localized.
2D. Glucagonoma (Necrolytic Migratory Erythema - NME)
  • Secretes Glucagon → Hyperglycemia & characteristic skin rash.
  • Symptoms:
  • Necrolytic Migratory Erythema (NME) → Painful, erythematous rash (legs, groin, face).
  • Diabetes Mellitus (mild to moderate).
  • Weight loss, anemia, stomatitis.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum glucagon >500 pg/mL.
  • CT/EUS for tumor localization.
  • Management:
  • Surgical resection if localized.
  • Somatostatin analogs (octreotide) for symptom control.
2E. Somatostatinoma
  • Secretes Somatostatin → Inhibits multiple hormones & digestive functions.
  • Symptoms:
  • Diabetes (↓ insulin).
  • Steatorrhea & malabsorption (↓ pancreatic enzymes & bile).
  • Achlorhydria (↓ acid secretion).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum somatostatin >30 pg/mL.
  • CT/EUS for tumor localization.
  • Management:
  • Surgical resection if localized.
  • Somatostatin analogs for symptom relief.
